glance.label: Main Idea
glance.html: Proverbs 16 places every human plan, word, and decision under the LORD who weighs the spirits and directs each step, and it gathers around that truth sayings on the righteous king, pride before a fall, gracious speech, the troublemaker, and self-control.

glance.label: Setting
glance.html: Chapter 16 opens the second part of Solomon’s collection (16:1–22:16), right after 15:33 joined the fear of the LORD to humility. More sayings now develop one thought across both lines, and the LORD’s rule frames the chapter (16:1, 33).

glance.label: Key Verse
glance.html: “A man’s heart plans his way, But the LORD directs his steps.” (Proverbs 16:9)

cards.title: The Heart of the Chapter
cards.html:
Proverbs 16 begins and ends with the same truth. People really do plan, for “The preparations of the heart belong to man” (16:1), yet the answer that comes from the tongue, the steps a man actually takes, and even the lot cast into the lap all belong to the LORD (16:1, 9, 33). He “weighs the spirits” (16:2), measuring motives a person cannot see clearly in himself, and so the wise commit their works to Him (16:3). This opening cluster also reaches what no plan can repair. “In mercy and truth Atonement is provided for iniquity” (16:6); it is God’s provision, and mercy and truth meet fully in Christ, through whom “grace and truth came” (John 1:17).

The rest of the chapter shows the LORD’s rule touching ordinary life. A king’s throne “is established by righteousness” (16:12), and honest scales are the LORD’s own work (16:11). Pride, the heart claiming a place that belongs to God, “goes before destruction” (16:18). Speech follows the heart: pleasant words heal like honey (16:24), while the ungodly man’s lips burn like fire (16:27). The chapter ranks the man “who rules his spirit” above the one who takes a city (16:32).

cards.title: Chapter Sections
cards.html:
Proverbs 16:1–9 — The LORD Directs Human Plans

The LORD gives the answer of the tongue, weighs motives that look pure to their owner, steadies the thoughts of those who entrust their works to Him, and keeps even the wicked within His purpose for the day of doom. Pride stands condemned, atonement comes in mercy and truth with turning from evil following it, and the section ends where it began, with a man planning his way while the LORD directs his steps.

Proverbs 16:10–15 — The King’s Righteous Rule

Because the king’s verdict carries decisive authority, his mouth must not betray justice, and his throne stands only on righteousness, just as honest scales belong to the LORD. A good king prizes honest speech, a wise man knows how to calm his wrath, and his favor brings life like the spring rain that ripens the harvest.

Proverbs 16:16–24 — Wisdom, Humility, and Pleasant Words

Wisdom is worth more than gold, the upright keep to a highway that leads away from evil, and a humble place among the lowly is better than a share of the proud man’s plunder, since pride runs ahead of a fall. Trust in the LORD brings true happiness, and a wise heart teaches the mouth to speak words that, like a honeycomb, sweeten the soul and strengthen the body.

Proverbs 16:25–30 — The Way of Death and the Troublemaker

The way that only seems right, first heard at 14:12, returns at the head of this section, followed by the laborer whose hunger keeps him working. Then comes a portrait of the troublemaker, who digs up evil, sows strife, parts close friends with whispering, lures his neighbor into a bad way, and gives away his plots with a wink and pursed lips.

Proverbs 16:31–33 — Gray Hair, Self-Control, and the Lot

Gray hair is a crown of glory when it is found in a righteous life, and mastery of one’s own temper outranks the strength that captures a city. The last word returns to the LORD: the lot falls into the lap, yet its every decision is His.

cards.title: Why This Chapter Matters
cards.html:
Proverbs 16 keeps planning and trust together. No saying here tells anyone to stop preparing; the chapter places his plans under a God who weighs motives and directs steps (16:2, 9). Committing one’s works to the LORD steadies the planner without guaranteeing that every venture succeeds, and the saying about enemies made to be at peace (16:7) describes His gracious working, not a shield against all opposition.

The chapter also exposes pride at its root. The proud heart is an abomination to the LORD (16:5), and its fall is the end of refusing to see itself rightly before Him (16:18). The fear of the LORD turns a person from evil (16:6) and leaves him content to stand “with the lowly” (16:19). Humility is a right view of oneself before God, very different from self-contempt.

cards.title: Key Themes to Watch For
cards.html:
The LORD’s rule over human plans. People plan, speak, and cast lots, but the outcome and the steps belong to Him (16:1, 3, 9, 33).

Motives weighed. Ways that look pure to their owner are measured by the LORD, who detests a proud heart however many allies it gathers (16:2, 5).

Righteous rule. Kings are to judge justly, hate wickedness, and value honest lips, because a throne rests on righteousness (16:10–15). These sayings speak first of Israel’s kings, and Scripture’s promise of a King who rules “with judgment and justice” forever finds its answer in Christ (Isaiah 9:7).

Pride and humility. Pride is the road to a fall, and a humble spirit among the lowly is worth more than any spoil (16:5, 18–19).

Words that come from the heart. The wise heart teaches the mouth and pleasant words heal, while the ungodly man’s speech burns and the whisperer separates friends (16:21, 23–24, 27–28).

cards.title: Key Words & Concepts
cards.html:
Weighs the spirits (16:2). The picture is of a merchant’s scale. The LORD measures the motives behind a person’s actions, so self-approval is never the final verdict.

Commit (16:3). The Hebrew verb pictures rolling a burden onto another. To commit one’s works to the LORD is to entrust them and their outcome to Him.

Even the wicked for the day of doom (16:4). Everything the LORD made serves His purpose, and wickedness never escapes His rule or His judgment. The verse does not make God the author of evil, for He has “no pleasure in the death of one who dies” (Ezekiel 18:32).

Mercy and truth (16:6). In Hebrew, hesed and emet: the LORD’s steadfast love and faithfulness, though some read them as a person’s own loyalty and faithfulness. Either way, atonement is God’s provision, and the psalmist sings, “Mercy and truth have met together” (Psalm 85:10).

Divination (16:10). The word usually names a practice God forbids (compare Deuteronomy 18:10). Here it describes the decisive authority of the king’s verdict and gives no approval to divination.

The lot (16:33). Casting lots was a way Israel sought the LORD’s decision (compare Acts 1:26). The saying places even what looks like chance under His rule and gives no approval to gambling.

sections.title: The Way of Death and the Troublemaker
Gray Hair, Self-Control, and the Lot

1.brief: A new group of sayings opens with the LORD’s rule over human plans. People make their preparations in their hearts, but the answer that finally comes from the tongue is from the LORD, so even what we end up saying lies within His rule.
1.explain:
“The preparations of the heart belong to man,”

Proverbs 16 opens a new movement in Solomon’s sayings, and its first word is about the LORD’s rule over human plans. The first line gives people their real part. The preparations of the heart, the arranging and ordering of thoughts and plans, belong to man. People think ahead, set things in order, and decide what they mean to say and do. The saying does not dismiss that work or call it pointless.

“But the answer of the tongue is from the LORD.”

Yet the answer that finally comes from the tongue is from the LORD. A person may prepare his words carefully, but what he actually ends up saying, and the outcome it produces, lies within God’s rule. The line probably includes both the words that are finally spoken and the final verdict on any matter. Either way, the last word belongs to God. Proverbs says the same of all human planning: “There are many plans in a man’s heart, Nevertheless the LORD’s counsel—that will stand” (19:21). The two lines set human responsibility and God’s sovereignty side by side without letting either cancel the other, and the rest of 16:1–9 develops that theme.
1.notes:
ESV and NASB render “preparations” as “plans,” and YLT as “arrangements.” The Hebrew word describes what the heart sets in order ahead of time, the thinking-through that the first line credits to man.

The phrase “from the LORD” in 16:1 returns in 16:33, “its every decision is from the LORD,” so the chapter opens and closes with the same confession.

2.brief: People tend to judge their own ways as pure, seeing their motives in the best light. The LORD weighs the spirits, measuring the motives behind the actions, so self-approval is never the final verdict.
2.explain:
“All the ways of a man are pure in his own eyes,”

People tend to judge their own ways kindly. A person sees his actions in the best light, explains his motives generously, and finds himself innocent. “Pure in his own eyes” is the verdict nearly everyone gives himself. The saying does not say a man’s ways are pure; it says they look pure to him.

“But the LORD weighs the spirits.”

The LORD weighs the spirits. The picture is of a merchant’s scale, measuring exactly what something is worth. God measures the motives behind the actions, the inner person that a man cannot see clearly in himself. Self-approval is never the final verdict. This is why the fear of the LORD humbles a person: it reminds him that the One who weighs the heart sees what he cannot. Proverbs repeats the thought with slightly different words: “Every way of a man is right in his own eyes, But the LORD weighs the hearts” (21:2).
2.notes:
The Hebrew verb behind “weighs” pictures weighing something out on a scale. NASB renders “spirits” as “motives,” the inner reasons God measures.

KJV and NASB read “clean” for “pure.”

3.brief: Committing one’s works to the LORD means entrusting them to Him and leaving the outcome in His hands. When a person does that, his thoughts and plans are established and made steady, which is God’s steadying of the planner rather than a guarantee that every undertaking will succeed.
3.explain:
“Commit your works to the LORD,”

This saying is a command. To commit one’s works to the LORD is to roll them onto Him, to entrust both the work and its outcome to His hands. The person still works; the command assumes real effort and real undertakings. But he no longer carries the weight of the result alone. The psalmist uses the same picture: “Commit your way to the LORD, Trust also in Him, And He shall bring it to pass” (Psalm 37:5).

“And your thoughts will be established.”

When a person entrusts his works to God, his thoughts will be established, made firm and steady. His thoughts here are his plans and purposes. Note what is promised and what is not. The works are committed; the thoughts are established. God steadies the planner and brings his purposes into line with His own. The verse does not promise that every undertaking will succeed as the person intended. It promises that the one who places his works in God’s hands will find his plans set on a firm footing, under the God who directs his steps (16:9).
3.notes: The Hebrew behind “Commit” is literally “Roll,” as YLT renders it: the picture is of rolling a burden off oneself and onto the LORD.

4.brief: Everything the LORD made serves His purpose, and even the wicked do not escape it, for they are headed for the day of doom. The verse affirms that wickedness stays under God’s rule and will meet His judgment, without making God the author of evil, for He has no pleasure in the death of one who dies (Ezekiel 18:32).
4.explain:
“The LORD has made all for Himself,”

Everything the LORD made serves His purpose. Nothing in creation stands outside His plan or escapes His rule. The phrase “for Himself” can also be read as for its purpose, meaning that God has fitted each thing for its proper end. Either way, the world is not a random collection of events; God governs it and directs it toward His ends.

“Yes, even the wicked for the day of doom.”

Even the wicked are included. They do not escape God’s purpose, for they are headed for the day of doom, the day of disaster and judgment. The verse affirms that wickedness stays under God’s rule and will meet His judgment. It does not make God the author of evil or say that He delights in the destruction of the wicked. He says plainly, “I have no pleasure in the death of one who dies” (Ezekiel 18:32), and calls the wicked to turn and live. God is good, and His goodness includes His justice. Even the evil that people intend, He can turn toward His good purposes, as Joseph told his brothers: “you meant evil against me; but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). The verse should not be used on its own to build a doctrine of God creating people for destruction.
4.notes:
The Hebrew behind “for Himself” can mean for its answer or for its purpose; the noun is the same one translated “answer” in 16:1. ESV and NASB read “purpose,” while KJV, with NKJV, reads “for himself.”

The Hebrew behind “the day of doom” is literally the day of evil or disaster, as KJV and NASB render it.

5.brief: The LORD detests everyone who is proud in heart. Even if the proud join forces to protect one another, none of them will escape punishment, the same assurance 11:21 gave about the wicked.
5.explain:
“Everyone proud in heart is an abomination to the LORD;”

The LORD detests everyone who is proud in heart. The pride in view is not merely a proud look or proud words, but pride rooted in the heart, a settled self-exaltation that has no room for God. Among the seven things the LORD hates, the first is “A proud look” (6:17). Pride is at bottom a wrong view of God and of oneself, which is why the fear of the LORD, a right view of God, exposes it.

“Though they join forces, none will go unpunished.”

The proud may band together, supporting and protecting one another, but none of them will escape punishment. Their numbers cannot shield them from God’s judgment. The line repeats the assurance 11:21 gave about the wicked: “Though they join forces, the wicked will not go unpunished” (11:21). The saying belongs with the chapter’s longer treatment of pride in 16:18–19.
5.notes: The Hebrew behind “though they join forces” is literally hand to hand, which KJV renders as hand joining in hand. “Will not go unpunished” is literally will not be acquitted or held innocent, as YLT shows with “not acquitted.”

6.brief: In mercy and truth atonement is provided for iniquity, and the fear of the LORD leads a person to turn away from evil. Atonement is God’s provision, not something human kindness earns, and mercy and truth meet fully in Christ, for “grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17).
6.explain:
“In mercy and truth Atonement is provided for iniquity;”

This is one of the few places in Proverbs that speaks of atonement. The Hebrew verb comes from the root used for atonement in Israel’s sacrifices, the covering and removing of guilt. In mercy and truth, atonement is provided for iniquity. Mercy and truth are the LORD’s steadfast love and faithfulness, the qualities He shows in keeping His promises. Some read them as the person’s own loyalty and faithfulness, but even then atonement is God’s provision, not something human kindness earns. The psalmist sings, “Mercy and truth have met together” (Psalm 85:10), and in the fullness of time they met fully in Christ, for “grace and truth came through Jesus Christ” (John 1:17). God “made Him who knew no sin to be sin for us” (2 Corinthians 5:21).

“And by the fear of the LORD one departs from evil.”

The second line shows what follows atonement: the fear of the LORD leads a person to turn away from evil. Forgiveness and a changed life belong together. The person whose iniquity has been covered now sees God rightly and turns from what God hates. “Fear the LORD and depart from evil” (3:7). The verse does not make turning from evil the cause of atonement; it makes it the fruit.
6.notes:
ESV renders “mercy and truth” as steadfast love and faithfulness, and NASB as lovingkindness and truth. KJV says iniquity is “purged.” The Hebrew verb behind “atonement is provided” comes from the same root used throughout Leviticus for making atonement; here it is passive, so iniquity is atoned for, without any mention of sacrifice.

The Hebrew verb behind “atonement is provided” in 16:6 also appears in 16:14, where a wise man will “appease” the king’s wrath; there it means to pacify.

7.brief: When a person’s ways please the LORD, He can turn even enemies into people at peace with him. The LORD’s rule reaches into human relationships, though this describes His gracious working rather than a promise that the godly will never face opposition.
7.explain:
“When a man’s ways please the LORD,”

The saying begins with a person whose ways please the LORD. His life, not just his words or his worship, is acceptable to God. This is the person who has committed his works to the LORD (16:3) and walks in the fear of the LORD (16:6).

“He makes even his enemies to be at peace with him.”

The LORD can turn even enemies into people at peace with such a person. God’s rule reaches into human relationships. He can soften hearts, change circumstances, and bring reconciliation where it seemed impossible. Esau, who had once threatened to kill Jacob, “ran to meet him, and embraced him” (Genesis 33:4). Yet this describes God’s gracious working, not a promise that the godly will never face opposition. Jesus pleased the Father perfectly and still had enemies who crucified Him. The saying shows what God is able to do and often does, not what He must always do.
7.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “makes even his enemies to be at peace” is a causative form, meaning that someone causes the action: the LORD brings about peace. The verb comes from the same root as shalom, the Hebrew word for peace and wholeness. The NKJV’s capitalized “He” shows that the LORD is the one acting, while NLT makes it sound as if the enemies simply become peaceful.

8.brief: A little gained with righteousness is better than great income gained without justice. How wealth is gained matters more than how much of it there is.
8.explain:
“Better is a little with righteousness,”

A little gained and held with righteousness is better. The saying is another “better than” comparison, like 15:16. It sets a small portion honestly gained against a large one unjustly gained, and it puts the small portion first.

“Than vast revenues without justice.”

Vast revenues without justice are worse. Great income gained by cheating, oppression, or crooked dealing cannot match a little gained rightly. How wealth is gained matters more than how much of it there is. The saying fits the LORD’s rule over human plans: since He weighs the spirits (16:2) and makes all for Himself (16:4), unjust gain has no future, while a little with righteousness has His approval.
8.notes:
The Hebrew behind “without justice” uses the ordinary word for justice or right judgment, the same word translated “judgment” in 16:10. KJV reads “without right.”

Compare 15:16, “Better is a little with the fear of the LORD, Than great treasure with trouble.”

9.brief: Human beings really do plan, and a man’s heart maps out his way. Yet the LORD directs his steps, so planning and trust belong together, and neither cancels the other.
9.explain:
“A man’s heart plans his way,”

Human beings really do plan. A man’s heart thinks through his way, considers options, and maps out a route. Proverbs does not discourage planning; it commends counsel and forethought (15:22). The heart that plans is doing what God made it to do.

“But the LORD directs his steps.”

Yet the LORD directs his steps. The plan is the man’s, but the actual steps are guided and established by God. This does not cancel planning or make it pointless; it places planning within God’s rule. A person makes his plans and then trusts God to guide each step, knowing that God’s direction is better than his own. Jeremiah prayed, “It is not in man who walks to direct his own steps” (Jeremiah 10:23), and Proverbs asks, “How then can a man understand his own way?” (20:24). The verse sums up the section that began with 16:1: people plan, and the LORD rules.
9.notes:
“Directs” translates the same Hebrew verb rendered “established” in 16:3, which means to make firm. ESV reads “establishes.”

The words “heart,” “man,” and “the LORD” appear in both 16:1 and 16:9, framing the opening section on the LORD’s rule over human plans.

Proverbs 16:10–15 — The King’s Righteous Rule

10.brief: The king’s word carries the weight of an authoritative verdict, so his mouth must not betray justice when he judges. “Divination” here describes the decisive authority of his judgments, not approval of practices God forbids.
10.explain:
“Divination is on the lips of the king;”

A group of sayings about the king begins here (16:10–15). “Divination” usually names a practice God forbids; Israel was not to have among them “one who practices witchcraft” or one who “interprets omens” (Deuteronomy 18:10). Here the word is used in a striking way to describe the authority of the king’s verdict. When the king judges, his word settles the matter with the weight of a final decision, as if it came from above. The saying gives no approval to divination; it describes how decisive a king’s judgment is.

“His mouth must not transgress in judgment.”

Because the king’s word carries such weight, his mouth must not betray justice. A ruler whose verdicts are final has a heavy responsibility to judge rightly. Solomon himself asked God for “an understanding heart to judge Your people” (1 Kings 3:9), and when he judged wisely, all Israel “saw that the wisdom of God was in him to administer justice” (1 Kings 3:28). The royal sayings describe what an ordinary king ought to be: a judge whose verdicts are just. Isaiah’s picture of the Messiah’s throne, established “with judgment and justice” (Isaiah 9:7), shows that same duty perfectly fulfilled, though not every earthly king in these sayings is a picture of Christ.
10.notes:
The Hebrew word behind “Divination” is the ordinary word for divination. KJV softens it to a “divine sentence,” and ESV reads “An oracle.”

The Hebrew verb form in the second line can express either a statement or an obligation. ESV takes it as a statement, that his mouth does not sin in judgment, while the NKJV’s “must not” and NASB’s “should not” take it as an obligation. The obligation fits the sayings that follow, which assume that kings can fail.

11.brief: Honest weights and scales belong to the LORD, and every weight in the merchant’s bag is His work. Fair dealing is not a human invention but part of the LORD’s own order for the world.
11.explain:
“Honest weights and scales are the LORD’s;”

In the marketplace, goods were weighed on a balance scale against stone weights. A dishonest merchant could carry two sets of weights, one for buying and one for selling. The Law commanded, “You shall have honest scales, honest weights” (Leviticus 19:36). This saying goes further: honest weights and scales belong to the LORD. Fair measurement is His.

“All the weights in the bag are His work.”

Every weight in the merchant’s bag is God’s work. Fair dealing is not a human invention or a mere business rule; it is part of the LORD’s own order for the world. Proverbs says elsewhere, “Dishonest scales are an abomination to the LORD, But a just weight is His delight” (11:1). Placed among the royal sayings, this verse reminds rulers that justice in the marketplace is part of the justice they must uphold, because the standards themselves come from God.
11.notes:
The Hebrew behind “the weights in the bag” is literally the stones of the bag, because merchants carried stone weights in a pouch. Deuteronomy 25:13 forbids having “in your bag differing weights.”

ESV and NASB speak of a just balance and scales.

12.brief: Kings are to find wickedness detestable, because a throne stands firm only on righteousness. Power that rests on injustice undermines itself.
12.explain:
“It is an abomination for kings to commit wickedness,”

Kings are to find wickedness detestable, especially wickedness in their own conduct. A king who does evil disgraces his office. The line can also mean that good kings detest wickedness in others and will not tolerate it in their courts; both senses fit the picture of a ruler who stands firmly against evil.

“For a throne is established by righteousness.”

The reason follows: a throne stands firm only on righteousness. Power that rests on injustice undermines itself, while just rule brings stability. Proverbs repeats the principle: “Take away the wicked from before the king, And his throne will be established in righteousness” (25:5), and “The king who judges the poor with truth, His throne will be established forever” (29:14). A ruler’s security depends not on force but on justice.
12.notes:
The Hebrew of the first line says literally an abomination to kings is doing wickedness. The 1984 NIV takes it of kings detesting wrongdoing in others, while ESV and NASB, with the NKJV, speak of kings themselves doing evil.

“Established” translates the same Hebrew verb used in 16:3 and 16:9, meaning to be made firm.

13.brief: Good kings delight in righteous lips and love the one who speaks what is right. A wise ruler wants honest counsel, not flattery.
13.explain:
“Righteous lips are the delight of kings,”

Good kings delight in righteous lips, in advisers and servants who speak honestly. A wise ruler wants to hear the truth, even when it is unwelcome, because his decisions depend on accurate counsel. Flatterers tell him what he wants to hear; righteous lips tell him what he needs to know.

“And they love him who speaks what is right.”

Kings love the one who speaks what is right. The truthful counselor wins the ruler’s affection and trust. The saying describes the ideal king and, by implication, warns kings who prefer flattery. It also encourages those who serve under authority to speak honestly, trusting that a good ruler values the truth.
13.notes: NASB renders the second line in the passive, that the one who speaks right is loved.

14.brief: The king’s wrath is like a band of messengers sent to bring death. A wise man knows how to calm that anger, using wisdom to turn danger away.
14.explain:
“As messengers of death is the king’s wrath,”

The king’s anger is like messengers sent to bring death. In the ancient world, a king’s wrath could mean execution, and his officers carried out his sentence swiftly. The image warns of the danger of provoking a ruler. Proverbs says elsewhere, “The king’s wrath is like the roaring of a lion” (19:12).

“But a wise man will appease it.”

A wise man knows how to calm the king’s anger. He uses wisdom, patience, and fitting words to turn danger away. The wise man does not flatter or deceive; he speaks with understanding and helps the king see more clearly. The saying shows wisdom at work in the most dangerous setting, turning wrath into peace.
14.notes: The Hebrew verb behind “appease” is the same one used for atonement in 16:6. Here it has the sense of covering or pacifying anger, which is why KJV and YLT render it “pacify.”

15.brief: The light of the king’s face, his favor and approval, means life. His favor is like a cloud bringing the latter rain, the spring showers that ripen the harvest, so a righteous ruler’s favor brings refreshing to those under him.
15.explain:
“In the light of the king’s face is life,”

The light of the king’s face is his favor and approval, the bright, welcoming look of a ruler pleased with his servant. That favor means life: protection, provision, and opportunity. Where the king’s wrath brings death (16:14), his favor brings life.

“And his favor is like a cloud of the latter rain.”

The king’s favor is like a cloud bringing the latter rain, the spring showers that came before harvest and ripened the crops. God promised Israel “the early rain and the latter rain, that you may gather in your grain” (Deuteronomy 11:14). A righteous ruler’s favor brings refreshing and fruitfulness to those under him. The image of a shining face also recalls the priestly blessing, “The LORD make His face shine upon you” (Numbers 6:25), which places every earthly king’s favor beneath the favor of the King of kings.
15.notes:
The latter rain fell in spring, before the grain harvest. ESV and NASB render it “spring rain.”

A similar comparison appears in 19:12, “his favor is like dew on the grass.”

Proverbs 16:16–24 — Wisdom, Humility, and Pleasant Words

16.brief: Getting wisdom is far better than getting gold, and understanding is to be chosen over silver. The verse is an exclamation, pressing the reader to value what lasts above what merely glitters.
16.explain:
“How much better to get wisdom than gold!”

The verse is an exclamation, not a calm comparison. Getting wisdom is far better than getting gold. Gold was the most precious and lasting form of wealth, yet wisdom is worth more. Wisdom herself said, “My fruit is better than gold, yes, than fine gold” (8:19). Gold can buy many things, but it cannot teach a person how to live, and it can be lost in a day.

“And to get understanding is to be chosen rather than silver.”

Understanding is to be chosen over silver. The word “chosen” presses the reader to decide. Between silver and understanding, a person must pick, and the saying urges him to choose what lasts above what merely glitters. The verse follows the royal sayings and reminds kings and commoners alike that wisdom is the true treasure.
16.notes: The same comparison runs through the opening chapters: “For her proceeds are better than the profits of silver, And her gain than fine gold” (3:14), and “Receive my instruction, and not silver” (8:10).

17.brief: The upright travel a highway whose direction is away from evil. Keeping to that road guards one’s life, so staying on the right way is itself a form of protection.
17.explain:
“The highway of the upright is to depart from evil;”

The upright travel a highway, a raised and well-kept road, and its direction is away from evil. Their whole way of life is a steady turning from what is wrong. The highway image recalls 15:19, where “the way of the upright is a highway.” Departing from evil is not an occasional detour for them; it is the road itself.

“He who keeps his way preserves his soul.”

Keeping to that road guards one’s life. The person who watches his way, staying on the highway and not wandering off, preserves his soul. Staying on the right way is itself a form of protection. The saying echoes 13:3, where the one who guards his mouth “preserves his life.” Whether it is the mouth or the way, what a person guards guards him in return.
17.notes: NASB says the one who “watches” his way preserves his life.

18.brief: Pride goes before destruction, and a haughty spirit before a fall. This is the book’s central word on pride: the proud heart sets itself up for ruin because it will not see its need before God, and the fear of the LORD exposes that pride.
18.explain:
“Pride goes before destruction,”

This is the book’s central word on pride. Pride goes before destruction; it walks ahead of ruin and leads to it. The proud heart sets itself up for a fall because it will not see its need before God. It trusts its own judgment, refuses correction, and presumes on God and others. Pride is a heart issue that the fear of the LORD exposes, for “The fear of the LORD is to hate evil; Pride and arrogance and the evil way And the perverse mouth I hate” (8:13). Earlier sayings touched the same theme: “When pride comes, then comes shame” (11:2), and “By pride comes nothing but strife” (13:10).

“And a haughty spirit before a fall.”

A haughty spirit, a lofty, self-exalting attitude, goes before a fall. The second line restates the first with a slightly different image: the proud man is walking high and does not see where his feet are going. The familiar English saying about pride going before a fall blends the two lines, but the verse has both destruction and stumbling in view. Pride presumes, and the one who presumes on himself, on others, or on God is headed for a fall. The opposite is humility, a right view of oneself before God, which 16:19 commends.
18.notes:
NASB and YLT render “fall” as “stumbling.” The Hebrew word behind “destruction” means a breaking or shattering, the same word that describes the spirit broken by perverse speech in 15:4.

The thought returns in 18:12, “Before destruction the heart of a man is haughty, And before honor is humility,” and in 29:23, “A man’s pride will bring him low.”

19.brief: It is better to be humble in spirit and stand with the lowly than to share the plunder of the proud. Humility is a right view of oneself before God, and it is worth more than anything pride can win.
19.explain:
“Better to be of a humble spirit with the lowly,”

It is better to be humble in spirit and stand with the lowly. The lowly here are the humble and the poor, those without status or power. To be among them with a humble spirit means accepting a modest place and sharing their lot. Proverbs says that God “gives grace to the humble” (3:34), and humility is a right view of oneself before God, not self-contempt.

“Than to divide the spoil with the proud.”

It is worse to divide the spoil with the proud. The proud may win battles, gain plunder, and enjoy success, but sharing their gains means sharing their pride and its end. The “better than” comparison puts humility above anything pride can win. Following directly after 16:18, the verse shows the choice clearly: the proud are headed for destruction, so standing with the humble is safer and better, even if it means having less.
19.notes: The Hebrew word translated “lowly” describes the poor and afflicted, people of low standing. ESV and YLT read “the poor,” and NASB “the lowly.”

20.brief: The one who pays wise attention to the word will find good. The second line names where that good finally comes from: whoever trusts in the LORD is happy.
20.explain:
“He who heeds the word wisely will find good,”

The one who pays wise attention to the word will find good. The “word” may be God’s word or wise instruction more generally; in either case, the person who listens thoughtfully and acts on what he hears will find good results. Wisdom is not just hearing but heeding.

“And whoever trusts in the LORD, happy is he.”

The second line names where that good finally comes from: whoever trusts in the LORD is happy, truly blessed. Heeding the word and trusting the LORD belong together. The word directs the person, and trust rests his confidence in the God who gave it. The father urged his son at the start, “Trust in the LORD with all your heart, And lean not on your own understanding” (3:5). In a chapter about God’s rule over human plans, this verse shows the right response: listen wisely and trust Him.
20.notes:
The Hebrew word for “the word” can also mean a matter or affair. KJV speaks of handling a matter wisely, while ESV and NASB read “the word.”

“Happy is he” translates the same Hebrew declaration of blessing as in 14:21; ESV and NASB read “blessed.”

21.brief: A wise heart earns a reputation for discernment. Sweetness of the lips, gracious and pleasant speech, increases learning, because people receive more readily what is spoken kindly.
21.explain:
“The wise in heart will be called prudent,”

A wise heart earns a reputation for discernment. People recognize wisdom when they see it, and the wise in heart come to be known as prudent and understanding. The reputation follows the reality; it is not manufactured.

“And sweetness of the lips increases learning.”

Sweetness of the lips, gracious and pleasant speech, increases learning. People receive more readily what is spoken kindly. A wise person who speaks harshly may be right, but he will teach less than one who speaks graciously. The saying begins a short group of sayings on wise speech (16:21–24) and shows that how something is said affects how well it is received.
21.notes:
The Hebrew word behind “learning” can also mean persuasiveness, the power of teaching to win a hearing, as ESV and NASB render it. The same word describes the seductress’s “enticing speech” (7:21), so persuasive speech can serve wisdom or folly.

The same Hebrew word for “learning” returns in 16:23, “adds learning to his lips,” linking the two sayings.

22.brief: Understanding is a wellspring of life to the one who has it, a source that keeps refreshing him. For fools, folly itself becomes their correction, as their own foolishness brings its painful results.
22.explain:
“Understanding is a wellspring of life to him who has it.”

Understanding is a wellspring of life to the one who has it, a source that keeps flowing and refreshing him. The image matches “a fountain of life” used of the teaching of the wise (13:14) and the fear of the LORD (14:27). Understanding gives life to its owner, guiding him away from danger and toward what is good.

“But the correction of fools is folly.”

For fools, folly itself becomes their correction. Their own foolishness brings painful results, and those results correct them, often after they have refused the instruction others offered. The line may also mean that trying to correct fools is folly, since they will not learn, or that whatever instruction fools give is folly. The NKJV’s wording fits the first reading best: where understanding is a source of life, folly becomes its own punishment.
22.notes:
“Wellspring of life” translates the same Hebrew phrase rendered “fountain of life” in 13:14 and 14:27. ESV and NASB read “fountain of life.”

Translations take the second line in different directions. The 1984 NIV speaks of folly bringing punishment to fools, NLT says “discipline is wasted on fools,” and ESV speaks of the instruction of fools.

23.brief: The wise heart trains the mouth. What a wise person says flows from what his heart has learned, and so his words add learning to his lips.
23.explain:
“The heart of the wise teaches his mouth,”

The wise heart trains the mouth. What a wise person says flows from what his heart has learned. His heart is like a teacher instructing a student, so that his mouth speaks wisely. Words that come from a well-taught heart are trustworthy.

“And adds learning to his lips.”

The wise heart adds learning to his lips, making his speech richer and more persuasive. The more the heart grows in wisdom, the more the lips have to offer. The saying connects with 16:21, where sweetness of the lips increases learning, and with 15:28, where the heart of the righteous studies how to answer. Good speech begins in the heart.
23.notes: The Hebrew behind “teaches” is literally makes wise: the wise heart causes the mouth to act wisely, as YLT renders it. ESV and NASB render “learning” as “persuasiveness,” as in 16:21.

24.brief: Pleasant words are like a honeycomb, sweet to the soul and health to the bones. Kind and gracious speech does real good to the whole person who hears it.
24.explain:
“Pleasant words are like a honeycomb,”

Pleasant words are like a honeycomb, sweet and delightful. Honey was a prized sweetness in the ancient world, and a honeycomb dripping with it was a picture of delight. Kind and gracious words have that effect on those who hear them. The psalmist used the same image of God’s word: “Sweeter also than honey and the honeycomb” (Psalm 19:10).

“Sweetness to the soul and health to the bones.”

Such words are sweetness to the soul and health to the bones. They do good to the whole person, inner and outer. Gracious speech refreshes the spirit and even affects physical well-being. The saying closes the group on speech (16:21–24) with a picture of how much good kind words can do, in contrast with the burning words of the ungodly man in 16:27.
24.notes:
“Pleasant words” translates the same Hebrew expression, literally words of pleasantness, that appears in 15:26.

“Health” translates the Hebrew word for healing used in 13:17 and 15:4; NASB renders it “healing.”

Proverbs 16:25–30 — The Way of Death and the Troublemaker

25.brief: This saying repeats 14:12 word for word, now on the other side of the division at 16:1: a way can seem right and still end in death. The repetition presses home that sincerity alone does not keep a person safe.
25.explain:
“There is a way that seems right to a man,”

This saying repeats 14:12 word for word, now on the other side of the division at 16:1. A road can seem right to a man, straight and sensible from where he stands, and he can follow it with full confidence. The fuller treatment at 14:12 applies here as well.

“But its end is the way of death.”

The end of that road is death. The repetition presses home that sincerity alone does not keep a person safe. In its new setting the saying gains added force. Chapter 16 has just said that “All the ways of a man are pure in his own eyes” (16:2) and that “A man’s heart plans his way” (16:9). The way that seems right is the way a man plans for himself without the LORD who weighs the spirits and directs the steps. The saying also introduces the portraits of the troublemaker that follow (16:27–30), men whose ways lead others toward ruin.
25.notes: The NKJV text of 16:25 is identical to 14:12. The two fall on either side of the 16:1 boundary in the book’s structure.

26.brief: Hunger drives a laborer on, for his own mouth keeps him working. The need to eat is a spur to work that benefits the one who works.
26.explain:
“The person who labors, labors for himself,”

The worker works for himself, in the sense that his labor benefits him. The verse is a plain observation about why people work. Work meets the worker’s own needs, and that is a good and natural thing. The repetition of “labors” stresses that the effort and its benefit go together.

“For his hungry mouth drives him on.”

His hungry mouth drives him on. The need to eat is a spur to work. Hunger presses the laborer to keep going, and the result is that he provides for himself. The saying views this positively: God has built into human life a need that motivates honest work. Ecclesiastes says, “All the labor of man is for his mouth” (Ecclesiastes 6:7). Hunger keeps the worker from becoming the lazy man of 15:19, whose way is blocked by thorns.
26.notes: ESV and NASB speak of the worker’s “appetite” in the first line, where the NKJV has “the person who labors.” For “drives him on,” ESV and NASB say his hunger “urges” him, and YLT pictures his mouth making him bend over his work.

27.brief: An ungodly man digs up evil as if digging a pit, searching out harm to use against others. His words burn like a scorching fire, spreading damage wherever he speaks.
27.explain:
“An ungodly man digs up evil,”

The ungodly man is literally a worthless man, a man of Belial, a Hebrew expression for a corrupt, good-for-nothing troublemaker. He digs up evil as if digging a pit, searching out harm to use against others. He looks for scandal, faults, and secrets and brings them to the surface to do damage. Proverbs warns elsewhere, “Whoever digs a pit will fall into it” (26:27).

“And it is on his lips like a burning fire.”

His words burn like a scorching fire, spreading damage wherever he speaks. What he digs up, he speaks out, and his speech burns reputations, relationships, and communities. James uses the same image: “the tongue is a fire” (James 3:6). The saying begins a short portrait of the troublemaker (16:27–30): the worthless man, the perverse man, the whisperer, and the violent man. Each one does harm through words, influence, or schemes.
27.notes:
The Hebrew behind “An ungodly man” is literally a man of Belial, an expression for a worthless, good-for-nothing person; ESV and NASB render it “worthless.” A similar Hebrew description introduces the troublemaker of 6:12, “A worthless person, a wicked man.”

ESV renders “digs up” as “plots,” while NASB keeps “digs up.”

28.brief: A perverse man sows strife the way a farmer sows seed. A whisperer spreading gossip can separate even the closest friends, so a few quiet words can do lasting damage.
28.explain:
“A perverse man sows strife,”

A perverse man, someone who twists and turns things upside down, sows strife the way a farmer sows seed. He scatters discord, and it grows into quarrels and divisions. Among the seven things the LORD hates is “one who sows discord among brethren” (6:19).

“And a whisperer separates the best of friends.”

A whisperer, a gossip or talebearer, separates even the closest friends. A few quiet words in the right ear can destroy a friendship that took years to build. Proverbs says, “The words of a talebearer are like tasty trifles, And they go down into the inmost body” (18:8), and “he who repeats a matter separates friends” (17:9). The saying shows how much damage can come from small, secret words.
28.notes:
The Hebrew behind “sows” is literally sends out, as strife is sent out among people. “A perverse man” is literally a man of perversities.

The Hebrew word behind “whisperer” describes someone who murmurs or whispers against others. ESV keeps “whisperer,” and NASB has “slanderer.”

29.brief: A violent man works on his neighbor by enticement, drawing him into a way that is not good. Violence often recruits before it strikes, as the sinners of 1:10–19 did.
29.explain:
“A violent man entices his neighbor,”

A violent man works on his neighbor by enticement. He does not always strike directly; he first draws others in, persuading them to join him. Violence often recruits before it strikes, as the sinners of chapter 1 did: “My son, if sinners entice you, Do not consent” (1:10). The violent man needs companions, and he finds them among his neighbors.

“And leads him in a way that is not good.”

He leads his neighbor down a way that is not good. The neighbor may not intend evil at first, but he is drawn step by step onto a harmful path. The saying warns of the influence of violent people and connects with 13:20, where the companion of fools will be destroyed. The way the violent man offers may seem exciting or profitable, but its end is not good.
29.notes: “Entices” translates the same Hebrew verb used in 1:10, “if sinners entice you,” where the father warns his son against joining a violent gang. In both places it means to persuade someone toward wrongdoing.

30.brief: The troublemaker’s face betrays his plans: he winks his eye while plotting perverse things and purses his lips as he brings evil about. Small gestures can signal a heart set on harm.
30.explain:
“He winks his eye to devise perverse things;”

The troublemaker’s face betrays his plans. He winks his eye, or narrows or shuts it, while plotting perverse things. The gesture signals to an accomplice or reveals the scheming going on inside. Proverbs described the worthless man earlier: “He winks with his eyes, He shuffles his feet, He points with his fingers” (6:13).

“He purses his lips and brings about evil.”

He purses his lips as he brings evil about. The tight-lipped look of someone who has decided on harm marks the moment the plan becomes action. Small gestures can signal a heart set on harm. The saying closes the portrait of the troublemaker (16:27–30), showing how his inner scheming shows on his face and then becomes deeds.
30.notes:
KJV says he “shutteth” his eyes, and NASB renders “purses” as “compresses.”

Proverbs 16:31–33 — Gray Hair, Self-Control, and the Lot

31.brief: Silver hair is a crown of glory when it is found in the way of righteousness. The honor belongs to a long life lived well, not to age by itself, and the saying is not a promise of long life.
31.explain:
“The silver-haired head is a crown of glory,”

Silver hair is a crown of glory, a mark of honor. In Israel, gray hair was a sign of age and experience, and the aged were to be honored: “You shall rise before the gray headed” (Leviticus 19:32). A long life brings knowledge that cannot be gained any other way.

“If it is found in the way of righteousness.”

The honor belongs to a long life lived well, not to age by itself. Gray hair is glorious when it is found in the way of righteousness. An old person who has walked with God carries a crown; an old person who has lived wickedly carries only years. The saying is not a promise of long life to every righteous person, for many righteous people die young. It honors the righteous life that has reached old age. Proverbs says elsewhere, “the splendor of old men is their gray head” (20:29).
31.notes: The NKJV, like the KJV, reads the second line as a condition with “If.” ESV, NASB, and YLT read it as a statement of where the crown is found, in a righteous life.

32.brief: Mastering one’s own temper is greater than military might, and ruling one’s spirit is better than capturing a city. Self-control is a strength that wins the battle within.
32.explain:
“He who is slow to anger is better than the mighty,”

The person who is slow to anger is better than the mighty warrior. Patience and self-control are greater strengths than military power. A soldier may win battles, but a patient person wins the harder battle against his own temper.

“And he who rules his spirit than he who takes a city.”

Ruling one’s spirit is better than capturing a city. Conquering a city took strategy, courage, and force, yet mastering one’s own spirit is greater. The opposite picture appears later: “Whoever has no rule over his own spirit Is like a city broken down, without walls” (25:28). The person who cannot control himself is defenseless; the person who rules his spirit is stronger than any conqueror.

33.brief: The lot is cast into the lap, a practice Israel used when seeking God’s decision, yet every outcome is from the LORD (compare Acts 1:26). The chapter ends as it began, with nothing, not even what looks like chance, outside His rule, and the verse gives no approval to gambling or divination.
33.explain:
“The lot is cast into the lap,”

Casting lots was a way Israel sought God’s decision. The lot was cast into the lap, as the verse says, and the result was received as a decision. Joshua divided the land by lot “before the LORD” (Joshua 18:10), and the apostles cast lots to choose Matthias (Acts 1:26). The lot looked like chance, but it was used in prayer and trust.

“But its every decision is from the LORD.”

Every decision of the lot is from the LORD. Even what looks like chance lies under His rule. The chapter ends as it began, with the LORD’s sovereignty over human plans (16:1). People prepare, plan, cast lots, and make decisions, but the outcome is God’s. The verse describes a practice used in seeking God’s will in Israel; it gives no approval to gambling or to divination. Its point is that nothing, not even the smallest roll of a stone, falls outside God’s rule.
33.notes:
KJV speaks of the whole “disposing” of the lot. The Hebrew word behind “decision” is the ordinary word for judgment or verdict, the same word translated “justice” in 16:8. In 16:11 it stands behind “Honest” in “Honest weights and scales,” where the Hebrew reads literally a balance and scales of justice.

The phrase “from the LORD” links this verse with 16:1, framing the chapter.
